raw_case_text:
During the child's hospitalization, his mother, a 44-year-old female with mild hypertension, complained of malaise and fever, receiving treatment at the emergency department of the same hospital. On admission, she presented with a ten-day history of fever, chills, headache, myalgia, asthenia, and weight loss. She was diagnosed with hypotension (95x70 mmHg) in the emergency room, which resolved following intravenous rehydration. She was admitted to the adult intensive care unit without oxygen support or vasoactive drugs. Physical examination revealed mild jaundice and an enlarged liver and spleen. No changes in the respiratory or cardiac systems were observed.
Laboratory tests on admission revealed hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL; hematocrit 27.5%; leukocytes 4,670/mm3 (segmented 79%); platelets 47,000/microL; INR 1.0; C-reactive protein 151.2; total bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL (direct bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL); gamma-glutamyl transferase 86 U/L; blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 53 mg/dL; creatinine 1.6 mg/dL; glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase 38 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase 18 U/L; sodium 125 mEq/L, potassium 2.6 mEq/L; creatine phosphokinase (CPK) 188 U/L; lactate dehydrogenase 854 U/L. The SARS-CoV-2 RT-qPCR results were positive with a nasal swab. Chest computed tomography revealed small ground-glass opacities with less than 5% involvement and laminar pleural effusion.
 P. vivax was identified using a rapid malaria test and confirmed by microscopy and qPCR after genomic DNA extraction from slides (). A thin blood-smear examination identified 2078.15 parasites/microL of blood, parasitemia of two crosses. (Figure 1). A cytokine storm profile was identified () (Figures 2 and 3). 
Plasma levels of 29 cytokines were measured in P. vivax and SARS-CoV-2-co-infected patients (mother), P. vivax-infected patient (child), and healthy donors (control). Expression levels of interleukin (IL)-6, IL-10, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, IL-1RA, MIP-1a, interferon (IFN)-gamma, tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha, MIP-1b, IL-8, IL-1b, IP-10, IL-1a, IL-7, IL-13 were increased by  10-fold in the co-infected patient (mother) when compared with mean cytokine levels of the healthy donor and Plasmodium vivax-infected patient (child) (Figure 2); these findings are compatible with the cytokine storm signature of severe respiratory infection pathogenesis, as revealed by biological enrichment analysis using IPA software (https://digitalinsights.qiagen.com/IPA (Figure 3). 
Treatment with intravenous artesunate (2.4 mg/kg/dose at 0, 12, and 24 h) was initiated. After administering three parenteral doses and following parasitemia of  1%, treatment was changed to oral hydroxychloroquine 600 mg/day for three days and primaquine 30 mg/day for seven days. The patient subsequently recovered completely. 
The Research Ethics and Committee approved the publication of this work.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old female presenting with a 10-day history of fever, chills, headache, myalgia, asthenia, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 44-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a 10-day history of fever, chills, headache, generalized myalgias, asthenia, malaise, and weight loss while her 7-year-old son was hospitalized for severe febrile illness. In the emergency department, she was diagnosed with hypotension (95/70 mmHg) which stabilized after intravenous fluid resuscitation, and she was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of mild hypertension. Epidemiological exposure: resided in a peri-urban area of south Bahia, Brazil, neighboring a rural settlement with an ongoing confirmed malaria outbreak; contact with her son hospitalized for severe febrile illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, headache, myalgia, asthenia, malaise, and weight loss. Negative for cough, chest pain, or dyspnea. Home medications: antihypertensive therapy. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Blood pressure 95/70 mmHg on arrival, responsive to IV rehydration; afebrile post-rehydration, no vasoactive drugs or oxygen required. Sclerae showed mild jaundice. Abdominal examination revealed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Respiratory and cardiac examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory tests on admission: hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, hematocrit 27.5%, leukocytes 4,670/mm3 (79% segmented neutrophils), platelets 47,000/microL, INR 1.0, C-reactive protein 151.2 mg/L, total bilirubin 2.0 mg/dL (direct bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL), gamma-glutamyl transferase 86 U/L, BUN 53 mg/dL, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, AST/GOT 38 U/L, ALT 18 U/L, sodium 125 mEq/L, potassium 2.6 mEq/L, CPK 188 U/L, LDH 854 U/L. Nasopharyngeal swab SARS-CoV-2 RT-qPCR: positive. Peripheral blood smear performed.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest computed tomography (CT): small ground-glass opacities involving less than 5% of lung parenchyma and laminar pleural effusion. Cytokine storm profiling: marked >=10-fold upregulation of 14 plasma cytokines including IL-6, IL-10, G-CSF, IL-1RA, MIP-1a, IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha, MIP-1b, IL-8, IL-1b, IP-10, IL-1a, IL-7, and IL-13.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Plasmodium vivax malaria coinfection with SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), complicated by hypotension, acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and a systemic hyperinflammatory cytokine storm.
Diagnostic confirmation: Rapid diagnostic test positive for Plasmodium vivax; confirmed by thin blood smear microscopy demonstrating 2,078.15 parasites/microL (two crosses parasitemia) and qPCR; positive nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 RT-qPCR.
Treatment & Outcome: Admitted to ICU and rehydrated with intravenous fluids. Treated with intravenous artesunate (2.4 mg/kg/dose at 0, 12, and 24 hours); after three parenteral doses and reduction of parasitemia to <1%, therapy was transitioned to oral hydroxychloroquine 600 mg/day for 3 days and primaquine 30 mg/day for 7 days. Recovered completely with resolution of acute renal dysfunction, electrolyte derangements, and thrombocytopenia.
